# Appendices and Technical Background {#sec-appendices}

This appendix provides essential technical results and mathematical foundations that support the main chapters of these tutorials. The
material is organized into three main sections: technical lemmas and inequalities used in learning theory proofs
(@sec-tech-lemmas), a comprehensive review of linear algebra concepts (@sec-linear-algebra-recap), and fundamental concentration
inequalities from probability theory (@sec-measure-concentration).

These results are referenced throughout these tutorials, particularly in @sec-learning-theory where we establish generalization bounds,
and in @sec-supervised-learning where we analyze algorithm convergence. Readers encountering unfamiliar mathematical concepts in
the main chapters should consult the relevant sections here for detailed definitions and proofs. Every statement is followed by
examples and exercises with hidden solutions, and the chapter closes with three exercises that combine its sections.

## Technical Lemmas and Inequalities {#sec-tech-lemmas}

This appendix presents fundamental technical lemmas and inequalities that are frequently used throughout these tutorials. These results
provide the mathematical foundation for many of the theoretical guarantees and convergence analyses in machine learning theory.

### Basic Algebraic Lemmas

The following lemmas establish relationships between logarithmic and linear functions that are essential for deriving sample
complexity bounds. The first one says how large $x$ must be before the linear function $x$ overtakes $a\log(x)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-log-versus-linear}
#### Logarithm versus linear growth

Let $a > 0$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then: $x \geq 2a\log(a) \Rightarrow x \geq a\log(x)$. It follows that a necessary
condition for the inequality $x < a\log(x)$ to hold is that $x < 2a\log(a)$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* First note that for $a \in (0, \sqrt{e}]$ the inequality $x \geq a\log(x)$ holds unconditionally and therefore the claim
is trivial. From now on, assume that $a > \sqrt{e}$. Consider the function $f(x) = x - a\log(x)$. The derivative is $f'(x) = 1 -
a/x$. Thus, for $x > a$ the derivative is positive and the function increases. In addition,

$$ \begin{aligned} f(2a\log(a)) &= 2a\log(a) - a\log(2a\log(a)) \\ &= 2a\log(a) - a\log(a) - a\log(2\log(a)) \\ &= a\log(a) -
a\log(2\log(a)) \end{aligned} $$

Since $a - 2\log(a) > 0$ for all $a > 0$, the proof follows. $\square$

This lemma is particularly useful when analyzing the relationship between sample size and VC dimension in PAC learning bounds.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest way to see @lem-app-log-versus-linear at work is to fix a value of $a$ and compare both sides numerically. The
example also shows the second half of the lemma, a value of $x$ below the threshold where $x < a\log(x)$ indeed holds.

::: {#exm-app-log-versus-linear-numeric}
#### The threshold for $a = 10$

With natural logarithms and $a = 10$, the threshold is $2a\log(a) = 20\log 10 \approx 46.05$. For $x = 47$ we get
$a\log(x) = 10\log 47 \approx 38.50 \leq 47$, as the lemma promises. For $x = 30$ we get $10\log 30 \approx 34.01 > 30$, so
$x < a\log(x)$ holds there, and consistently with the necessary condition, $30 < 46.05$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
In learning theory the lemma is applied with $a$ equal to a dimension divided by an accuracy. The exercise below asks for the
resulting explicit sample size in one concrete case, and for a direct check that it works.

::: {#exr-app-log-versus-linear-sample-size}
#### An explicit sample size

Let $d = 5$ and $\epsilon = 0.1$. Use @lem-app-log-versus-linear to find an integer $m_0$ such that every $m \geq m_0$ satisfies
$m \geq (d/\epsilon)\log(m)$, and check the inequality directly at $m = m_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $a = d/\epsilon = 50$. The lemma says that $m \geq 2a\log(a) = 100\log 50 \approx 391.2$ implies $m \geq 50\log(m)$, so
$m_0 = 392$ works. Directly, $50\log 392 \approx 50 \cdot 5.971 = 298.6 \leq 392$.
:::
::::

The second lemma adds a constant offset $b$ to the logarithmic term, which is the form in which agnostic sample complexity bounds
appear. Its proof reduces it to @lem-app-log-versus-linear by splitting $x$ into two halves.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-log-versus-linear-offset}
#### Logarithm plus offset versus linear growth

Let $a \geq 1$ and $b > 0$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then: $x \geq 4a\log(2a) + 2b \Rightarrow x \geq a\log(x) + b$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* It suffices to prove that $x \geq 4a\log(2a) + 2b$ implies that both $x \geq 2a\log(x)$ and $x \geq 2b$. Since we assume
$a \geq 1$ we clearly have that $x \geq 2b$. In addition, since $b > 0$ we have that $x \geq 4a\log(2a)$ which using
@lem-app-log-versus-linear implies that $x \geq 2a\log(x)$. This concludes our proof. $\square$

This result is used to simplify sample complexity expressions in agnostic PAC learning.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest admissible parameters make @lem-app-log-versus-linear-offset easy to check by hand. The example evaluates the
threshold for $a = b = 1$ and confirms the conclusion at the first integer above it.

::: {#exm-app-log-versus-linear-offset-unit}
#### The case $a = b = 1$

The threshold is $4\log 2 + 2 \approx 4.77$. At $x = 5$ we have $\log 5 + 1 \approx 2.61 \leq 5$, as claimed.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The threshold of the lemma is sufficient but not necessary, and it is worth seeing by how much it overshoots. The exercise
computes it for a larger pair $(a, b)$ and tests a value well below it.

::: {#exr-app-log-versus-linear-offset-sharpness}
#### How sharp is the threshold?

Let $a = 10$ and $b = 20$. (a) Compute the threshold of @lem-app-log-versus-linear-offset and verify the conclusion at the next
integer. (b) Check whether $x = 80$ also satisfies $x \geq a\log(x) + b$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $4a\log(2a) + 2b = 40\log 20 + 40 \approx 119.83 + 40 = 159.83$. At $x = 160$, $10\log 160 + 20 \approx 50.75 + 20 = 70.75 \leq
160$. (b) $10\log 80 + 20 \approx 43.82 + 20 = 63.82 \leq 80$, so $x = 80$ satisfies the inequality as well: the threshold is
off by a factor of two or more, which is the price of the simple closed form.
:::
::::

### Concentration Lemmas

The following lemmas relate tail bounds to expectations, which are crucial for deriving generalization bounds. The first one
turns a sub-Gaussian tail with constant $2$ into a bound on the mean absolute deviation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation}
#### Expectation from a sub-Gaussian tail

Let $X$ be a random variable and $x' \in \mathbb{R}$ be a scalar and assume that there exists $a >
0$ such that for all $t \geq 0$ we have $\mathbb{P}[|X - x'| > t] \leq 2e^{-t^2/a^2}$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then,
$\mathbb{E}[|X - x'|] \leq 4a$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* For all $i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ denote $t_i = ai$. Since $t_i$ is monotonically increasing we have that $\mathbb{E}[|X -
x'|]$ is at most $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} t_i \mathbb{P}[|X - x'| > t_{i-1}]$. Combining this with the assumption in the lemma we get
that $\mathbb{E}[|X - x'|] \leq 2a\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} ie^{-(i-1)^2}$. The proof now follows from the inequalities

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} ie^{-(i-1)^2} \leq \sum_{i=1}^{5} ie^{-(i-1)^2} + \int_5^{\infty} xe^{-(x-1)^2}dx < 1.8 + 10^{-7} < 2 $$

$\square$

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Gaussian distribution is the model case of a sub-Gaussian tail, so it is the natural first test of
@lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation. Comparing the bound with the exact mean absolute value shows how generous the constant $4$ is.

::: {#exm-app-subgaussian-tail-gaussian}
#### A centred Gaussian

Let $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ and $x' = 0$. The Gaussian tail bound $\mathbb{P}[|X| > t] \leq 2e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ is the
hypothesis of the lemma with $a = \sqrt{2}\sigma$, so $\mathbb{E}[|X|] \leq 4\sqrt{2}\sigma \approx 5.66\sigma$. The exact value is
$\mathbb{E}[|X|] = \sigma\sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.80\sigma$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Bounded random variables also have sub-Gaussian tails, although the constant $a$ has to be found by hand. The exercise does this
for a uniform variable and compares the lemma with the exact mean.

::: {#exr-app-subgaussian-tail-uniform}
#### A uniform variable

Let $X$ be uniform on $[-1, 1]$ and $x' = 0$. Show that the hypothesis of @lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation holds with $a = 1$,
and compare the resulting bound with $\mathbb{E}[|X|]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $t \geq 1$ the tail is $0$. For $t \in [0, 1]$ it is $\mathbb{P}[|X| > t] = 1 - t$, and we need $1 - t \leq 2e^{-t^2}$. For
$t \geq 0.27$ we have $1 - t \leq 0.73 \leq 2e^{-1} \leq 2e^{-t^2}$; for $t < 0.27$ we have $2e^{-t^2} \geq 2e^{-0.073} > 1 \geq 1
- t$. So the lemma applies with $a = 1$ and gives $\mathbb{E}[|X|] \leq 4$, whereas $\mathbb{E}[|X|] = 1/2$.
:::
::::

A union bound over many events multiplies the tail by their number, so the constant in front of the exponential is no longer $2$.
The next lemma handles a prefactor $2b$ and pays for it with an additive $\sqrt{\log(b)}$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation-prefactor}
#### Expectation from a sub-Gaussian tail with a prefactor

Let $X$ be a random variable and $x' \in \mathbb{R}$ be a scalar and assume that there exists $a >
0$ and $b \geq e$ such that for all $t \geq 0$ we have $\mathbb{P}[|X - x'| > t] \leq 2be^{-t^2/a^2}$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then,
$\mathbb{E}[|X - x'|] \leq a(2 + \sqrt{\log(b)})$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* For all $i = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ denote $t_i = a(i + \sqrt{\log(b)})$. Since $t_i$ is monotonically increasing we have that

$$ \mathbb{E}[|X - x'|] \leq a\sqrt{\log(b)} + \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} t_i \mathbb{P}[|X - x'| > t_{i-1}] $$

Using the assumption in the lemma we have

$$ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} t_i \mathbb{P}[|X - x'| > t_{i-1}] &\leq 2ab\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} (i +
\sqrt{\log(b)})e^{-(i-1+\sqrt{\log(b)})^2} \\ &\leq 2ab\int_{1+\sqrt{\log(b)}}^{\infty} xe^{-(x-1)^2}dx \\ &=
2ab\int_{\sqrt{\log(b)}}^{\infty} (y+1)e^{-y^2}dy \\ &\leq 4ab\int_{\sqrt{\log(b)}}^{\infty} ye^{-y^2}dy \\ &=
2ab[-e^{-y^2}]_{\sqrt{\log(b)}}^{\infty} \\ &= 2ab/b = 2a \end{aligned} $$

Combining the preceding inequalities we conclude our proof. $\square$

This lemma is essential for analyzing Rademacher complexity and deriving data-dependent generalization bounds.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The typical source of the prefactor $b$ is a maximum over finitely many sub-Gaussian variables. The example shows how
@lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation-prefactor turns a union bound into the familiar $\sqrt{\log N}$ growth of the expected maximum.

::: {#exm-app-subgaussian-tail-maximum}
#### The maximum of $N$ sub-Gaussian variables

Let $X_1, \ldots, X_N$, with $N \geq 3$, each satisfy $\mathbb{P}[|X_j| > t] \leq 2e^{-t^2/a^2}$, and let $Y = \max_j |X_j|$. By the
union bound $\mathbb{P}[Y > t] \leq 2Ne^{-t^2/a^2}$, which is the hypothesis of the lemma with $x' = 0$ and $b = N \geq e$. Hence
$\mathbb{E}[\max_j |X_j|] \leq a(2 + \sqrt{\log N})$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The dependence on $b$ is only through $\sqrt{\log(b)}$, which grows very slowly. The exercise makes this concrete and asks why the
previous lemma could not be used instead.

::: {#exr-app-subgaussian-tail-maximum-growth}
#### Slow growth in the number of variables

In the setting of the previous example with $a = 1$, evaluate the bound for $N = 10^3$ and $N = 10^6$. Why does
@lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation not apply to $Y$ directly?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $N = 10^3$, $\log N \approx 6.91$ and the bound is $2 + 2.63 = 4.63$. For $N = 10^6$, $\log N \approx 13.82$ and the bound is $2
+ 3.72 = 5.72$: a thousandfold increase in $N$ adds about $1.1$. The earlier lemma needs the tail to be at most $2e^{-t^2/a^2}$ for
every $t \geq 0$, and the union bound only gives $2Ne^{-t^2/a^2}$, which is larger.
:::
::::

### Combinatorial Lemmas

The growth function of a hypothesis class of VC dimension $d$ is bounded by a partial sum of binomial coefficients, and that sum
must be compared with a polynomial in $m$. The next lemma gives the comparison in closed form.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-binomial-partial-sum}
#### Partial sums of binomial coefficients

Let $m, d$ be two positive integers such that $d \leq m - 2$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then,

$$ \sum_{k=0}^{d} \binom{m}{k} \leq \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d $$
:::

::::

*Proof.* We prove the claim by induction. For $d = 1$ the left-hand side equals $1 + m$ while the right-hand side equals $em$;
hence the claim is true. Assume that the claim holds for $d$ and let us prove it for $d + 1$. By the induction assumption we have

$$ \begin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^{d+1} \binom{m}{k} &\leq \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d + \binom{m}{d+1} \\ &=
\left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \left(1 + \left(\frac{d}{em}\right)^d \frac{m(m-1)(m-2)\cdots(m-d)}{(d+1)d!}\right) \\ &\leq
\left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \left(1 + \left(\frac{d}{e}\right)^d \frac{(m-d)}{(d+1)d!}\right) \end{aligned} $$

Using Stirling's approximation we further have that

$$ \begin{aligned} &\leq \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \left(1 + \left(\frac{d}{e}\right)^d \frac{(m-d)}{(d+1)\sqrt{2\pi
d}(d/e)^d}\right) \\ &= \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \left(1 + \frac{m-d}{\sqrt{2\pi d}(d+1)}\right) \\ &=
\left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot \frac{d+1+(m-d)/\sqrt{2\pi d}}{d+1} \\ &\leq \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot
\frac{d+1+(m-d)/2}{d+1} \\ &= \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot \frac{d/2+1+m/2}{d+1} \\ &\leq \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot
\frac{m}{d+1} \end{aligned} $$

where in the last inequality we used the assumption that $d \leq m - 2$. On the other hand,

$$ \begin{aligned} \left(\frac{em}{d+1}\right)^{d+1} &= \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot \frac{em}{d+1} \cdot
\left(\frac{d}{d+1}\right)^d \\ &= \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot \frac{em}{d+1} \cdot \frac{1}{(1+1/d)^d} \\ &\geq
\left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot \frac{em}{d+1} \cdot \frac{1}{e} \\ &= \left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d \cdot \frac{m}{d+1}
\end{aligned} $$

which proves our inductive argument. $\square$

This lemma provides the key bound on growth functions used in Sauer's lemma and VC dimension analysis.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A small case lets both sides of @lem-app-binomial-partial-sum be computed exactly. The example takes $m = 10$ and $d = 3$, which
satisfies the hypothesis $d \leq m - 2$.

::: {#exm-app-binomial-partial-sum-small}
#### $m = 10$, $d = 3$

The left-hand side is $1 + 10 + 45 + 120 = 176$ and the right-hand side is $(10e/3)^3 \approx 9.06^3 \approx 744$, so the
inequality holds with room to spare.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sauer's lemma bounds the growth function $\tau_{\mathcal{H}}(m)$ of a class of VC dimension $d$ by the partial binomial sum. The
exercise compares the exact sum, its polynomial bound and the trivial bound $2^m$ in one case.

::: {#exr-app-binomial-partial-sum-growth}
#### Polynomial versus exponential growth

Let $d = 2$ and $m = 20$. Compute $\sum_{k=0}^{2}\binom{20}{k}$, its bound from @lem-app-binomial-partial-sum, and $2^{20}$, and
compare their logarithms.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The sum is $1 + 20 + 190 = 211$, with $\log 211 \approx 5.35$. The bound is $(20e/2)^2 = (10e)^2 \approx 738.9$, with logarithm
$2\log(10e) \approx 6.61$. The trivial bound $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ has logarithm $20\log 2 \approx 13.86$. The polynomial bound
grows like $d\log m$, the trivial one like $m$.
:::
::::

### Exponential Inequalities

Hoeffding's inequality rests on bounding the moment generating function of a bounded variable, and the symmetric $\pm 1$ case comes
down to comparing the hyperbolic cosine with a Gaussian. The next lemma is that comparison.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-cosh-gaussian-bound}
#### Hyperbolic cosine bound

For all $a \in \mathbb{R}$ we have [@shalev2014ml]

$$ \frac{e^a + e^{-a}}{2} \leq e^{a^2/2} $$
:::

::::

*Proof.* Observe that

$$ e^a = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{a^n}{n!} $$

Therefore,

$$ \frac{e^a + e^{-a}}{2} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{a^{2n}}{(2n)!} $$

and

$$ e^{a^2/2} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{a^{2n}}{2^n n!} $$

Observing that $(2n)! \geq 2^n n!$ for every $n \geq 0$ we conclude our proof. $\square$

This inequality is fundamental in deriving Hoeffding's inequality and other concentration bounds.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Evaluating both sides of @lem-app-cosh-gaussian-bound at two points shows that the inequality is tight near $0$ and loose for large
$|a|$. This is the reason the resulting tail bounds are good for small deviations.

::: {#exm-app-cosh-gaussian-bound-values}
#### Two numerical values

At $a = 1$: $\cosh 1 \approx 1.543 \leq e^{1/2} \approx 1.649$. At $a = 2$: $\cosh 2 \approx 3.762 \leq e^{2} \approx 7.389$. Both
sides have the expansion $1 + a^2/2 + O(a^4)$, so they agree to second order at $a = 0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercise uses the lemma for what it was made for: a tail bound for a sum of random signs. It anticipates Markov's inequality
(@lem-app-markov) and Hoeffding's inequality (@lem-app-hoeffding-inequality) from @sec-measure-concentration.

::: {#exr-app-cosh-gaussian-bound-rademacher}
#### Sums of random signs

Let $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_m$ be independent with $\mathbb{P}[\sigma_i = 1] = \mathbb{P}[\sigma_i = -1] = 1/2$ and $S =
\sum_i \sigma_i$. Show that $\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda S}] \leq e^{m\lambda^2/2}$ for every $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and deduce that
$\mathbb{P}[S \geq t] \leq e^{-t^2/(2m)}$ for $t > 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By independence $\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda S}] = \prod_i \mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\sigma_i}] = (\cosh\lambda)^m \leq e^{m\lambda^2/2}$ by
@lem-app-cosh-gaussian-bound. For $\lambda > 0$, Markov's inequality applied to $e^{\lambda S}$ gives $\mathbb{P}[S \geq t] =
\mathbb{P}[e^{\lambda S} \geq e^{\lambda t}] \leq e^{-\lambda t + m\lambda^2/2}$. The exponent is minimised at $\lambda = t/m$,
which gives $e^{-t^2/(2m)}$.
:::
::::

## Linear Algebra Recap {#sec-linear-algebra-recap}

This section provides a comprehensive review of linear algebra concepts that are essential for understanding machine learning
algorithms and their theoretical foundations. We focus on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and present key definitions,
theorems, and decompositions. These results complement the linear algebra introduction in @sec-linear-algebra and provide the
technical details needed for understanding matrix decompositions, optimization algorithms, and dimensionality reduction techniques
discussed in @sec-supervised-learning and @sec-unsupervised-learning.

For more on this topic, see @zhao2025rl [Appendix].

### Basic Definitions and Notation

In these tutorials, we work exclusively with linear algebra over finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. Vectors are treated as column
vectors unless otherwise specified. The first definition fixes how lengths and angles are measured.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-inner-product-norms}
#### Inner products and norms

Given two $d$-dimensional vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, their inner product is
defined as

$$ \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{d} u_i v_i $$

The Euclidean norm (also called the $\ell_2$ norm) is $\|\mathbf{u}\| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u} \rangle}$. We also
frequently use the $\ell_1$ norm, $\|\mathbf{u}\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{d} |u_i|$, and the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm,
$\|\mathbf{u}\|_{\infty} = \max_i |u_i|$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A single vector with small integer entries already shows that the three norms of @def-app-inner-product-norms differ. The example
also computes one inner product.

::: {#exm-app-inner-product-norms-vector}
#### Three norms of one vector

Let $\mathbf{u} = (1, -2, 2)$ and $\mathbf{v} = (3, 0, -1)$. Then $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 3 + 0 - 2 = 1$,
$\|\mathbf{u}\| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$, $\|\mathbf{u}\|_1 = 5$ and $\|\mathbf{u}\|_{\infty} = 2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The ordering seen in the example is no accident. The exercise asks for the chain of inequalities between the three norms, which is
used whenever a bound in one norm is converted into another.

::: {#exr-app-inner-product-norms-comparison}
#### Comparing the norms

Show that $\|\mathbf{u}\|_{\infty} \leq \|\mathbf{u}\| \leq \|\mathbf{u}\|_1 \leq \sqrt{d}\,\|\mathbf{u}\|$ for every $\mathbf{u}
\in \mathbb{R}^d$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\max_i u_i^2 \leq \sum_i u_i^2$ gives the first inequality. Expanding $(\sum_i |u_i|)^2 = \sum_i u_i^2 + \sum_{i \neq j}
|u_i||u_j| \geq \sum_i u_i^2$ gives the second. For the third, apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to the vectors $(|u_1|, \ldots,
|u_d|)$ and $(1, \ldots, 1)$: $\sum_i |u_i| \leq \|\mathbf{u}\| \sqrt{d}$.
:::
::::

With lengths in place, the next notion describes the flat sets through the origin that vectors generate. Subspaces are the
ranges, null spaces and eigenspaces met later in this section.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-subspace-span}
#### Subspaces and span

A subspace of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that is closed under addition and scalar
multiplication. The span of a set of vectors $\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_k$ is the subspace containing all vectors of the
form

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i \mathbf{u}_i $$

where for all $i$, $\alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The span of two non-parallel vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a plane, and @def-app-subspace-span lets one find its equation. The
example does this for two simple vectors.

::: {#exm-app-subspace-span-plane}
#### A plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$

The span of $(1, 0, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 1)$ consists of the vectors $\alpha(1, 0, 1) + \beta(0, 1, 1) = (\alpha, \beta, \alpha +
\beta)$, that is, of the vectors with $z = x + y$: the plane $x + y - z = 0$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Deciding whether a set is a subspace means checking the two closure properties, and a half-space shows how one of them can fail.
The exercise contrasts it with the set of vectors orthogonal to a fixed one.

::: {#exr-app-subspace-span-check}
#### Hyperplanes and half-spaces

Fix $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Show that $\{\mathbf{u} : \langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{u} \rangle = 0\}$ is a subspace and that
$\{\mathbf{u} : u_1 \geq 0\}$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{u} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$, then $\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{u} +
\mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$ and $\langle \mathbf{w}, \alpha\mathbf{u} \rangle = 0$ by linearity of the inner product, so the first set
is a subspace. The second is closed under addition but not under multiplication by $-1$: $(1, 0, \ldots, 0)$ belongs to it and
$(-1, 0, \ldots, 0)$ does not.
:::
::::

A span can be generated by redundant vectors. The next definition removes the redundancy and so gives the notion of dimension.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-independence-basis}
#### Linear independence and bases

A set of vectors $U = \{\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_k\}$ is independent if for every $i$,
$\mathbf{u}_i$ is not in the span of $\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_{i-1}, \mathbf{u}_{i+1}, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_k$. We say that
$U$ spans a subspace $V$ if $V$ is the span of the vectors in $U$. We say that $U$ is a basis of $V$ if it is both independent and
spans $V$. The dimension of $V$ is the size of a basis of $V$, and it can be verified that all bases of $V$ have the same size
[@shalev2014ml].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The example shows a spanning set that is not independent and how removing one vector turns it into a basis. It illustrates
@def-app-independence-basis in the plane, where everything can be checked by eye.

::: {#exm-app-independence-basis-plane}
#### A redundant spanning set

The vectors $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, 1)$ span $\mathbb{R}^2$ but are not independent, since $(1, 1) = (1, 0) + (0, 1)$. Removing
$(1, 1)$ leaves the standard basis, so $\mathbb{R}^2$ has dimension $2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Verifying a basis means checking independence and spanning separately. The exercise does both for three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$,
finding explicit coordinates along the way.

::: {#exr-app-independence-basis-check}
#### A basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$

Show that $(1, 1, 0)$, $(1, 0, 1)$, $(0, 1, 1)$ form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Spanning: for $(x, y, z)$ put $\alpha = (x + y - z)/2$, $\beta = (x - y + z)/2$, $\gamma = (-x + y + z)/2$; then $\alpha(1, 1, 0) +
\beta(1, 0, 1) + \gamma(0, 1, 1) = (\alpha + \beta, \alpha + \gamma, \beta + \gamma) = (x, y, z)$. Independence: if one vector were
in the span of the other two, moving it to the other side would give a vanishing combination with not all coefficients zero. But
$\alpha + \beta = \alpha + \gamma = \beta + \gamma = 0$ forces $\beta = \gamma = -\alpha$ and $-2\alpha = 0$, so all coefficients
vanish.
:::
::::

Among all bases, those made of mutually perpendicular unit vectors are the most convenient, because coordinates are then inner
products. The next definition names them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-orthogonality}
#### Orthogonality

We say that $U$ is an orthogonal set if for all $i \neq j$, $\langle \mathbf{u}_i, \mathbf{u}_j \rangle = 0$.
We say that $U$ is an orthonormal set if it is orthogonal and if for every $i$, $\|\mathbf{u}_i\| = 1$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The standard basis is orthonormal, but so is any rotated copy of it. The example of @def-app-orthogonality is the basis rotated by
$45^\circ$, which reappears as the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix below.

::: {#exm-app-orthogonality-rotated}
#### A rotated orthonormal basis

The vectors $(1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$ have inner product $(1 - 1)/2 = 0$ and norm $1$, so they form an orthonormal
set, and hence a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The example used the fact that orthonormal vectors are independent. The exercise asks for its proof, which works for any orthogonal
set of nonzero vectors.

::: {#exr-app-orthogonality-independent}
#### Orthogonal sets are independent

Show that an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors is independent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Suppose $\mathbf{u}_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j \mathbf{u}_j$. Taking the inner product with $\mathbf{u}_i$ gives
$\|\mathbf{u}_i\|^2 = \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j \langle \mathbf{u}_j, \mathbf{u}_i \rangle = 0$, so $\mathbf{u}_i = \mathbf{0}$, a
contradiction.
:::
::::

Matrices act on vectors, and the subspaces attached to a matrix describe what it reaches and what it kills. The next definition
names these subspaces, the rank, and the transpose.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-range-null-rank}
#### Range, null space, rank and transpose

Given a matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, the range of $A$ is the span of its columns and the null
space of $A$ is the subspace of all vectors that satisfy $A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$. The rank of $A$ is the dimension of its
range.

The transpose of a matrix $A$, denoted $A^{\top}$, is the matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry equals the $(j,i)$ entry of $A$. We say that
$A$ is symmetric if $A = A^{\top}$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A matrix whose rows are proportional has a one-dimensional range and a large null space. The example computes both for a
$2 \times 3$ matrix, illustrating every notion of @def-app-range-null-rank.

::: {#exm-app-range-null-rank-proportional}
#### A rank-one matrix

Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$. Every column is a multiple of $(1, 2)$, so the range is the line
spanned by $(1, 2)$ and the rank is $1$. The null space is the plane $u_1 + 2u_2 + 3u_3 = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, of dimension $2$.
$A$ is not symmetric (it is not even square); $A^{\top}$ is the $3 \times 2$ matrix with rows $(1, 2)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 6)$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The matrix $A^{\top}A$ appears in least squares and in the singular value decomposition below. The exercise shows that it is
symmetric and has the same null space as $A$.

::: {#exr-app-range-null-rank-gram}
#### The null space of $A^{\top}A$

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$. Show that $A^{\top}A$ is symmetric and that its null space equals the null space of $A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(A^{\top}A)^{\top} = A^{\top}(A^{\top})^{\top} = A^{\top}A$. If $A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ then $A^{\top}A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$.
Conversely, if $A^{\top}A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ then $0 = \langle \mathbf{u}, A^{\top}A\mathbf{u} \rangle = \langle A\mathbf{u},
A\mathbf{u} \rangle = \|A\mathbf{u}\|^2$, so $A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$.
:::
::::

### Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Eigenvalue decomposition is fundamental to understanding many machine learning algorithms, including principal component analysis
and spectral clustering. An eigenvector is a direction that a square matrix only stretches.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-eigenvector}
#### Eigenvalue and eigenvector

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ be a matrix. A nonzero vector $\mathbf{u}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with a
corresponding eigenvalue $\lambda$ if

$$ A\mathbf{u} = \lambda\mathbf{u} $$
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest non-diagonal symmetric matrix already has two eigenvectors along the diagonals. The example checks
@def-app-eigenvector for it directly.

::: {#exm-app-eigenvector-symmetric}
#### A symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $A(1, 1) = (3, 3) = 3(1, 1)$ and $A(1, -1) = (1, -1)$, so $(1, 1)$ is an
eigenvector with eigenvalue $3$ and $(1, -1)$ one with eigenvalue $1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Not every real matrix has a real eigenvector, which is why the spectral decomposition below assumes symmetry. The exercise checks
this for a rotation.

::: {#exr-app-eigenvector-rotation}
#### A rotation has no real eigenvector

Show that $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has no eigenvector in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R\mathbf{u} = \lambda\mathbf{u}$ reads $-u_2 = \lambda u_1$ and $u_1 = \lambda u_2$. Substituting, $u_1 = -\lambda^2 u_1$, so
$(1 + \lambda^2)u_1 = 0$ and $u_1 = 0$; then $-u_2 = \lambda u_1 = 0$, so $u_2 = 0$ as well. Hence $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$,
which is not an eigenvector.
:::
::::

For symmetric matrices the situation is as good as possible: there is a full orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. The spectral
decomposition states this and reads off the rank, range and null space from it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-app-spectral-decomposition}
#### Spectral decomposition

If $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is a symmetric matrix of rank $k$ [@shalev2014ml], then
there exists an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^d$, $\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_d$, such that each $\mathbf{u}_i$ is an
eigenvector of $A$. Furthermore, $A$ can be written as

$$ A = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^{\top} $$

where each $\lambda_i$ is the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_i$. This can be written equivalently as $A =
UDU^{\top}$, where the columns of $U$ are the vectors $\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_d$, and $D$ is a diagonal matrix with
$D_{i,i} = \lambda_i$ and for $i \neq j$, $D_{i,j} = 0$. Finally, the number of $\lambda_i$ which are nonzero is the rank of the
matrix, the eigenvectors which correspond to the nonzero eigenvalues span the range of $A$, and the eigenvectors which correspond
to zero eigenvalues span the null space of $A$.
:::

::::

This decomposition is central to understanding the geometry of quadratic forms and optimization landscapes in machine learning.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The matrix of the previous example can now be reassembled from its eigenvectors. The example verifies the sum formula of
@thm-app-spectral-decomposition and then looks at a singular matrix, where the statement about range and null space has content.

::: {#exm-app-spectral-decomposition-two-by-two}
#### Two $2 \times 2$ decompositions

With $\mathbf{u}_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$ and $\mathbf{u}_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$,
$$ 3\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{u}_1^{\top} + \mathbf{u}_2\mathbf{u}_2^{\top} = \frac{3}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} +
\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. $$
For $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ the same vectors are eigenvectors with eigenvalues $2$ and $0$: $B$ has rank
$1$, its range is spanned by $\mathbf{u}_1$ and its null space by $\mathbf{u}_2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The decomposition turns powers of a matrix into powers of numbers. The exercise proves this and uses it to compute a cube without
multiplying matrices three times.

::: {#exr-app-spectral-decomposition-powers}
#### Powers of a symmetric matrix

Show that $A^k = \sum_i \lambda_i^k \mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{u}_i^{\top}$ for every integer $k \geq 1$, and compute $\begin{pmatrix} 2 &
1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Orthonormality gives $(\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{u}_i^{\top})(\mathbf{u}_j\mathbf{u}_j^{\top}) = \langle \mathbf{u}_i, \mathbf{u}_j
\rangle \mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{u}_j^{\top}$, which is $\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{u}_i^{\top}$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise; multiplying out
$A^k$ and induction on $k$ give the formula. For the matrix above, $A^3 = \frac{27}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} +
\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 14 & 13 \\ 13 & 14 \end{pmatrix}$, which agrees with
$A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ multiplied by $A$.
:::
::::

### Positive Definite Matrices

Positive definite matrices play a crucial role in optimization theory and kernel methods. The definition below uses the
eigenvalues provided by the spectral decomposition.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-positive-definite}
#### Positive definite and semidefinite matrices

A symmetric matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is positive definite if all its eigenvalues are positive. $A$
is positive semidefinite if all its eigenvalues are nonnegative.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The three $2 \times 2$ matrices below fall into the three possible cases of @def-app-positive-definite. Their eigenvectors are
$(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ in each case, so only the eigenvalues need computing.

::: {#exm-app-positive-definite-three-cases}
#### Definite, semidefinite, indefinite

$\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3, 1$ and is positive definite. $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $2, 0$ and is positive semidefinite but not definite. $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$
has eigenvalues $3, -1$ and is neither.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercise turns the example into a one-parameter family and asks where the transitions happen. Such a family is the
correlation matrix of two standardised variables.

::: {#exr-app-positive-definite-family}
#### A correlation matrix

For which $c \in \mathbb{R}$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & c \\ c & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ positive definite, and for which is it positive
semidefinite?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The vectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ are eigenvectors with eigenvalues $1 + c$ and $1 - c$. Both are positive iff $|c| < 1$ and both
are nonnegative iff $|c| \leq 1$.
:::
::::

Eigenvalues are not always the easiest thing to compute, so it helps to know other descriptions of the same class of matrices.
The next theorem gives two more.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-app-psd-characterizations}
#### Characterizations of positive semidefiniteness

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ be a symmetric matrix [@shalev2014ml]. Then, the following are equivalent
definitions of positive semidefiniteness of $A$:

1. All the eigenvalues of $A$ are nonnegative.
2. For every vector $\mathbf{u}$, $\langle \mathbf{u}, A\mathbf{u} \rangle \geq 0$.
3. There exists a matrix $B$ such that $A = BB^{\top}$.
:::

::::

The second characterization is particularly useful in optimization, as it ensures that quadratic forms are convex. The third
characterization connects positive semidefiniteness to the existence of matrix factorizations, which is fundamental in kernel
methods and Gaussian processes.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a rank-one matrix all three conditions of @thm-app-psd-characterizations can be checked at a glance. The example does so for
the all-ones matrix.

::: {#exm-app-psd-characterizations-ones}
#### The all-ones matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: the eigenvalues are $2$ and $0$; $\langle \mathbf{u}, A\mathbf{u} \rangle
= (u_1 + u_2)^2 \geq 0$; and $A = BB^{\top}$ with $B$ the column $(1, 1)^{\top}$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Kernel methods rely on Gram matrices being positive semidefinite. The exercise proves it through two of the three
characterizations.

::: {#exr-app-psd-characterizations-gram}
#### Gram matrices

Let $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $K_{ij} = \langle \mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j \rangle$. Show that $K$ is
positive semidefinite using condition 3, and again using condition 2.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $X$ be the $n \times d$ matrix with rows $\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}$. Then $K = XX^{\top}$, which is condition 3 with $B = X$.
Directly, $\langle \mathbf{u}, K\mathbf{u} \rangle = \sum_{i,j} u_i u_j \langle \mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j \rangle = \|\sum_i u_i
\mathbf{x}_i\|^2 \geq 0$, which is condition 2.
:::
::::

### Singular Value Decomposition

The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) generalizes eigenvalue decomposition to non-square matrices and is fundamental to
dimensionality reduction techniques. Since a rectangular matrix maps one space to another, the eigenvector equation is replaced by
a pair of equations linking a vector in each space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-singular-vectors}
#### Singular values and vectors

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ be a matrix of rank $r$. Unit vectors $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and
$\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ are called right and left singular vectors of $A$ with corresponding singular value $\sigma > 0$ if

$$ A\mathbf{v} = \sigma\mathbf{u} \quad \text{and} \quad A^{\top}\mathbf{u} = \sigma\mathbf{v} $$
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a diagonal matrix the singular vectors are coordinate vectors, but a negative diagonal entry shows that left and right singular
vectors need not coincide. The example checks @def-app-singular-vectors for such a matrix.

::: {#exm-app-singular-vectors-diagonal}
#### A diagonal matrix with a negative entry

Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$. With $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{e}_1$: $A\mathbf{e}_1 =
3\mathbf{e}_1$ and $A^{\top}\mathbf{e}_1 = 3\mathbf{e}_1$, so $\sigma = 3$. With $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{e}_2$, $\mathbf{u} =
-\mathbf{e}_2$: $A\mathbf{e}_2 = 2(-\mathbf{e}_2)$ and $A^{\top}(-\mathbf{e}_2) = 2\mathbf{e}_2$, so $\sigma = 2$, although $-2$ is
the eigenvalue.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A single column vector is the simplest non-square matrix. The exercise finds its only singular triple directly from the definition.

::: {#exr-app-singular-vectors-column}
#### A column vector

Find a singular value and a pair of singular vectors of $A = (1, 2, 2)^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The only unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^1$ are $\pm 1$; take $\mathbf{v} = 1$. Then $A\mathbf{v} = (1, 2, 2)$ has norm $3$, so $\sigma
= 3$ and $\mathbf{u} = (1, 2, 2)/3$. Check: $A^{\top}\mathbf{u} = (1 + 4 + 4)/3 = 3 = \sigma\mathbf{v}$.
:::
::::

Once enough singular triples are known, the matrix can be rebuilt from them. The next lemma gives the reconstruction formula.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-svd-expansion}
#### Expansion in singular vectors

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ be a matrix of rank $r$ [@shalev2014ml]. Assume that $\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots,
\mathbf{v}_r$ is an orthonormal set of right singular vectors of $A$, $\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_r$ is an orthonormal set
of corresponding left singular vectors of $A$, and $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r$ are the corresponding singular values. Then,

$$ A = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^{\top} $$

It follows that if $U$ is a matrix whose columns are the $\mathbf{u}_i$'s, $V$ is a matrix whose columns are the $\mathbf{v}_i$'s,
and $D$ is a diagonal matrix with $D_{i,i} = \sigma_i$, then

$$ A = UDV^{\top} $$
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The diagonal matrix of the previous example can be reassembled from the two singular triples found there. The example checks
@lem-app-svd-expansion in this case.

::: {#exm-app-svd-expansion-diagonal}
#### Reassembling a diagonal matrix

$3\mathbf{e}_1\mathbf{e}_1^{\top} + 2(-\mathbf{e}_2)\mathbf{e}_2^{\top} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} +
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
For a rank-one matrix the expansion has a single term. The exercise finds it for a matrix that is not diagonal.

::: {#exr-app-svd-expansion-rank-one}
#### A rank-one matrix

Find the expansion of @lem-app-svd-expansion for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A$ has rank $1$. Take $\mathbf{v} = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$; then $A\mathbf{v} = (\sqrt{2}, 0)$, so $\sigma = \sqrt{2}$ and $\mathbf{u} =
(1, 0)$, and $A^{\top}\mathbf{u} = (1, 1) = \sqrt{2}\mathbf{v}$. Hence $A = \sqrt{2}\,\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^{\top} = \sqrt{2} \cdot
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::
::::

**Connection to Eigenvalues.** The singular values of $A$ are intimately related to the eigenvalues of $A^{\top}A$ and
$AA^{\top}$. The next lemma makes the relation precise, and it is how singular values are computed in practice.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-singular-eigen}
#### Singular vectors as eigenvectors

$\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}$ are right and left singular vectors of $A$ with singular value $\sigma$ if and
only if $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A^{\top}A$ with corresponding eigenvalue $\sigma^2$ and $\mathbf{u} =
\sigma^{-1}A\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $AA^{\top}$ with corresponding eigenvalue $\sigma^2$ [@shalev2014ml].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The rank-one matrix of the last exercise gives a quick check of @lem-app-singular-eigen. Both products $A^{\top}A$ and
$AA^{\top}$ are written out.

::: {#exm-app-singular-eigen-rank-one}
#### Both Gram matrices of a rank-one matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $A^{\top}A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvector
$(1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$ with eigenvalue $2 = \sigma^2$, and $AA^{\top} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvector
$(1, 0)$ with eigenvalue $2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The lemma reduces finding singular values to an eigenvalue problem of size $n$. The exercise uses it on a $3 \times 2$ matrix whose
SVD is assembled in a later example.

::: {#exr-app-singular-eigen-three-by-two}
#### Singular values of a $3 \times 2$ matrix

Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Use @lem-app-singular-eigen to find its singular values and
singular vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A^{\top}A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ with eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1,
1)/\sqrt{2}$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$. So $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{3}$, $\sigma_2 = 1$, $\mathbf{u}_1 = A\mathbf{v}_1/\sqrt{3}
= (1, 1, 2)/\sqrt{6}$ and $\mathbf{u}_2 = A\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1, 0)/\sqrt{2}$. As a check, $AA^{\top} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1
\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ maps $(1, 1, 2)$ to $(3, 3, 6)$.
:::
::::

**Construction of Singular Vectors.** The following result shows how to construct singular vectors through optimization. Each
vector maximises the stretch $\|A\mathbf{v}\|$ among unit vectors orthogonal to the previous ones.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-singular-vectors-variational}
#### Variational construction of singular vectors

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r$ [@shalev2014ml]. Define the following vectors:

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}_1 &= \arg\max_{\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n: \|\mathbf{v}\| = 1} \|A\mathbf{v}\| \\ \mathbf{v}_2 &=
\arg\max_{\substack{\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n: \|\mathbf{v}\| = 1 \\ \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}_1 \rangle = 0}}
\|A\mathbf{v}\| \\ &\vdots \\ \mathbf{v}_r &= \arg\max_{\substack{\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n: \|\mathbf{v}\| = 1 \\ \forall i <
r, \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}_i \rangle = 0}} \|A\mathbf{v}\| \end{aligned} $$

Then, $\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_r$ is an orthonormal set of right singular vectors of $A$.
:::

::::

This construction provides the foundation for principal component analysis, where we seek directions of maximum variance in data.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a diagonal matrix the maximisations of @lem-app-singular-vectors-variational can be done by inspection. The example shows the
greedy choice picking the coordinate axes in order of their stretch.

::: {#exm-app-singular-vectors-variational-diagonal}
#### A diagonal matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and a unit vector $\mathbf{v}$, $\|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 = 9v_1^2 + 4v_2^2 = 4 +
5v_1^2$, maximised at $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{e}_1$ with value $3$. The only unit vectors orthogonal to it are $\pm\mathbf{e}_2$,
giving $\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{e}_2$ with $\|A\mathbf{v}_2\| = 2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercise redoes the $3 \times 2$ example by optimisation rather than by eigenvalues. It should reproduce the same right singular
vectors.

::: {#exr-app-singular-vectors-variational-three-by-two}
#### Maximising the stretch

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, find $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of
@lem-app-singular-vectors-variational.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For a unit vector, $\|A\mathbf{v}\|^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2 + (v_1 + v_2)^2 = 2 + 2v_1v_2$. Since $2v_1v_2 \leq v_1^2 + v_2^2 = 1$ with
equality iff $v_1 = v_2$, the maximum $3$ is attained at $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$, so $\|A\mathbf{v}_1\| = \sqrt{3}$. The
unit vectors orthogonal to it are $\pm(1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$, giving $\mathbf{v}_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$ with $\|A\mathbf{v}_2\|^2 = 2 - 1
= 1$.
:::
::::

The preceding lemmas combine into the existence of the decomposition for every matrix. The SVD theorem collects them and states
how the factors relate to the eigen-decompositions of $A^{\top}A$ and $AA^{\top}$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-app-svd}
#### SVD theorem

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ with rank $r$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then $A = UDV^{\top}$ where $D$ is
an $r \times r$ matrix with nonzero singular values of $A$ and the columns of $U, V$ are orthonormal left and right singular
vectors of $A$. Furthermore, for all $i$, $D_{i,i}^2$ is an eigenvalue of $A^{\top}A$, the $i$-th column of $V$ is the
corresponding eigenvector of $A^{\top}A$, and the $i$-th column of $U$ is the corresponding eigenvector of $AA^{\top}$.
:::

::::

The SVD is fundamental to many machine learning techniques including:

- Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction
- Low-rank matrix approximation and matrix completion
- Latent semantic analysis in natural language processing
- Recommender systems based on collaborative filtering
- Image compression and denoising

The optimality properties of SVD make it a cornerstone of modern data analysis and machine learning.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The singular triples of the $3 \times 2$ matrix found in the exercises above can now be assembled into its full decomposition. The
example multiplies the factors of @thm-app-svd back together.

::: {#exm-app-svd-three-by-two}
#### The SVD of a $3 \times 2$ matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ take $U = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{6} & 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{6} &
-1/\sqrt{2} \\ 2/\sqrt{6} & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $D = \operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{3}, 1)$ and $V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 &
1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. Then
$$ UDV^{\top} = \sqrt{3}\,\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^{\top} + \mathbf{u}_2\mathbf{v}_2^{\top} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1
& 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = A. $$
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
When $A$ has rank one, $D$ is a $1 \times 1$ matrix and the decomposition is a single outer product. The exercise computes it via
the eigenvectors of $A^{\top}A$, as the theorem prescribes.

::: {#exr-app-svd-rank-one}
#### A rank-one SVD

Compute the SVD of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ in the form of @thm-app-svd.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A^{\top}A = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ has the single nonzero eigenvalue $25$ with eigenvector $\mathbf{v} =
\mathbf{e}_1$, so $r = 1$, $D = (5)$, $V = \mathbf{e}_1$ and $U = A\mathbf{e}_1/5 = (3/5, 4/5)^{\top}$. Indeed $UDV^{\top} = 5 \cdot
(3/5, 4/5)^{\top}(1, 0) = A$.
:::
::::

### Additional Linear Algebra Topics

For matrices, we can define various norms. The two below measure the size of a matrix entrywise and as an operator, and both are
used to state approximation and convergence results.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-matrix-norms}
#### Matrix norms and operator norms

The Frobenius norm of a matrix $A \in
\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is defined as

$$ \|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}^2} $$

The operator norm (or spectral norm) is defined as

$$ \|A\|_2 = \max_{\|\mathbf{x}\|=1} \|A\mathbf{x}\| $$

which equals the largest singular value of $A$ [@deisenroth2020mml].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The $3 \times 2$ matrix whose SVD was computed above has known singular values, so both norms of @def-app-matrix-norms are
immediate. The example compares them.

::: {#exm-app-matrix-norms-three-by-two}
#### Both norms of one matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $\|A\|_F = \sqrt{4} = 2$ and $\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1 = \sqrt{3}$. Note
that $\|A\|_F^2 = 4 = 3 + 1 = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The example suggests that the Frobenius norm dominates the operator norm. The exercise proves this for every matrix with the
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

::: {#exr-app-matrix-norms-comparison}
#### Operator norm versus Frobenius norm

Show that $\|A\|_2 \leq \|A\|_F$ for every $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $\mathbf{a}_i$ be the $i$-th row of $A$ and $\|\mathbf{x}\| = 1$. Then $\|A\mathbf{x}\|^2 = \sum_i \langle \mathbf{a}_i,
\mathbf{x} \rangle^2 \leq \sum_i \|\mathbf{a}_i\|^2\|\mathbf{x}\|^2 = \|A\|_F^2$. Taking the maximum over $\mathbf{x}$ gives the
claim.
:::
::::

Two numbers attached to a square matrix, the trace and the determinant, are sums and products of its eigenvalues. The definition
below fixes both.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-app-trace-determinant}
#### Trace and determinant

The trace of a square matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is the sum of its diagonal elements:

$$ \text{tr}(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii} $$
:::

::::

The trace has the cyclic property: $\text{tr}(ABC) = \text{tr}(CAB) = \text{tr}(BCA)$. The determinant of $A$ is the product of
its eigenvalues and provides information about the volume scaling induced by the linear transformation.

These linear algebra concepts form the mathematical foundation for understanding optimization algorithms, dimensionality reduction
techniques, and the geometry of high-dimensional spaces in machine learning.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The symmetric matrix used throughout this section has eigenvalues $3$ and $1$. The example checks that its trace from
@def-app-trace-determinant and its determinant agree with their sum and product.

::: {#exm-app-trace-determinant-symmetric}
#### Trace and determinant of a symmetric matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $\text{tr}(A) = 4 = 3 + 1$ and $\det A = 4 - 1 = 3 = 3 \cdot 1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The cyclic property of the trace links the Frobenius norm to the singular values. The exercise proves the identity seen in the
example on matrix norms.

::: {#exr-app-trace-determinant-frobenius}
#### Frobenius norm and singular values

Show that $\|A\|_F^2 = \text{tr}(A^{\top}A)$ and, using @thm-app-svd and the cyclic property, that $\|A\|_F^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $(j, j)$ entry of $A^{\top}A$ is $\sum_i a_{ij}^2$, so $\text{tr}(A^{\top}A) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}^2 = \|A\|_F^2$. With $A =
UDV^{\top}$ and $U^{\top}U = I_r$, $A^{\top}A = VD^2V^{\top}$, and $\text{tr}(VD^2V^{\top}) = \text{tr}(D^2V^{\top}V) =
\text{tr}(D^2) = \sum_i \sigma_i^2$ since $V^{\top}V = I_r$.
:::
::::

## Measure Concentration and Probability Inequalities {#sec-measure-concentration}

Measure concentration inequalities quantify the deviation of empirical averages from their expectations when the sample size is
finite. These inequalities are fundamental to statistical learning theory and provide the basis for generalization bounds in
machine learning [@shalev2014ml; @zhao2025rl]. The results in this section are used extensively in @sec-learning-theory to derive
PAC learning bounds and in @sec-supervised-learning to analyze the convergence of learning algorithms.

Let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_m$ be an i.i.d. sequence of random variables and let $\mu$ be their mean. The strong law of large numbers
states that when $m$ tends to infinity, the empirical average, $\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} Z_i$, converges to the expected value
$\mu$, with probability 1. Measure concentration inequalities quantify this deviation for finite $m$.

### Markov's Inequality

We start with Markov's inequality, which provides a basic bound for nonnegative random variables. It uses nothing but the mean, and
every later inequality of this section is obtained by applying it to a suitable function of the variable.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-markov}
#### Markov's inequality

Let $Z$ be a nonnegative random variable. Then for every $a > 0$, $\mathbb{P}[Z \geq a] \leq \mathbb{E}[Z]/a$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* Let $Z$ be a nonnegative random
variable. The expectation of $Z$ can be written as:

$$ \mathbb{E}[Z] = \int_{x=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}[Z \geq x]dx $$

Since $\mathbb{P}[Z \geq x]$ is monotonically nonincreasing we obtain

$$ \forall a \geq 0, \quad \mathbb{E}[Z] \geq \int_{x=0}^{a} \mathbb{P}[Z \geq x]dx \geq \int_{x=0}^{a} \mathbb{P}[Z \geq a]dx =
a\mathbb{P}[Z \geq a] $$

Rearranging the inequality yields Markov's inequality:

$$ \forall a \geq 0, \quad \mathbb{P}[Z \geq a] \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[Z]}{a} $$

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
An exponential variable has an explicit tail, which lets one see how far @lem-app-markov is from the truth. The comparison
explains why sharper inequalities are needed later.

::: {#exm-app-markov-exponential}
#### An exponential variable

Let $Z$ be exponential with $\mathbb{E}[Z] = 1$, so $\mathbb{P}[Z \geq a] = e^{-a}$. At $a = 3$ Markov gives $1/3$, while the true
value is $e^{-3} \approx 0.050$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Although Markov's inequality is loose for the exponential distribution, it cannot be improved in general. The exercise exhibits a
variable for which it is an equality.

::: {#exr-app-markov-tight}
#### Markov's inequality is tight

Fix $a > 0$ and $p \in [0, 1]$. Find a nonnegative $Z$ with $\mathbb{P}[Z \geq a] = \mathbb{E}[Z]/a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $Z = a$ with probability $p$ and $Z = 0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[Z] = ap$ and $\mathbb{P}[Z \geq a] = p = \mathbb{E}[Z]/a$.
:::
::::

For variables confined to $[0,1]$, Markov's inequality can also be turned around to give lower bounds on the probability of being
large. This is the form used to show that a learner with small expected error has small error with reasonable probability.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-markov-bounded}
#### Markov's inequality for bounded variables

Let $Z$ be a random variable that takes values in $[0,1]$ [@shalev2014ml].
Assume that $\mathbb{E}[Z] = \mu$. Then, for any $a \in (0,1)$,

$$ \mathbb{P}[Z > 1-a] \geq \frac{\mu - (1-a)}{a} $$

This also implies that for every $a \in (0,1)$,

$$ \mathbb{P}[Z > a] \geq \frac{\mu - a}{1-a} \geq \mu - a $$
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A two-point variable with a large mean shows the lower bounds of @lem-app-markov-bounded in action. Both inequalities of the lemma
are evaluated for it.

::: {#exm-app-markov-bounded-two-point}
#### A two-point variable

Let $Z = 1$ with probability $0.9$ and $Z = 0$ otherwise, so $\mu = 0.9$. With $a = 0.2$: $\mathbb{P}[Z > 0.8] = 0.9 \geq (0.9 -
0.8)/0.2 = 0.5$, and $\mathbb{P}[Z > 0.2] = 0.9 \geq (0.9 - 0.2)/0.8 = 0.875 \geq 0.7$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The lemma is stated without proof above, and its proof is a one-line application of Markov's inequality. The exercise asks for it.

::: {#exr-app-markov-bounded-proof}
#### Proof via $1 - Z$

Prove @lem-app-markov-bounded by applying @lem-app-markov to $1 - Z$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$Y = 1 - Z$ is nonnegative with $\mathbb{E}[Y] = 1 - \mu$, so $\mathbb{P}[Z \leq 1 - a] = \mathbb{P}[Y \geq a] \leq (1 - \mu)/a$
and $\mathbb{P}[Z > 1 - a] \geq 1 - (1 - \mu)/a = (\mu - (1 - a))/a$. Replacing $a$ by $1 - a$ gives $\mathbb{P}[Z > a] \geq (\mu -
a)/(1 - a)$. If $\mu \geq a$, dividing the nonnegative number $\mu - a$ by $1 - a \in (0, 1)$ can only increase it, so this is at
least $\mu - a$. If $\mu < a$, then $\mathbb{P}[Z > a] \geq 0 > \mu - a$ trivially, so $\mathbb{P}[Z > a] \geq \mu - a$ holds in
all cases.
:::
::::

### Chebyshev's Inequality

Markov's inequality applied to the squared deviation brings the variance into play. The resulting bound is two-sided and
decreases like the inverse square of the deviation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-chebyshev}
#### Chebyshev's inequality

Let $Z$ be a random variable with finite variance. Then for every $a > 0$, $\mathbb{P}[|Z - \mathbb{E}[Z]| \geq a] \leq
\text{Var}[Z]/a^2$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* Applying Markov's inequality on the random variable $(Z - \mathbb{E}[Z])^2$ we obtain Chebyshev's inequality:

$$ \forall a > 0, \quad \mathbb{P}[|Z - \mathbb{E}[Z]| \geq a] = \mathbb{P}[(Z - \mathbb{E}[Z])^2 \geq a^2] \leq
\frac{\text{Var}[Z]}{a^2} $$

where $\text{Var}[Z] = \mathbb{E}[(Z - \mathbb{E}[Z])^2]$ is the variance of $Z$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A fair die is the simplest variable for which @lem-app-chebyshev can be compared with the exact probability. The example uses a
deviation that picks out the two extreme faces.

::: {#exm-app-chebyshev-die}
#### A fair die

For a fair die, $\mathbb{E}[Z] = 3.5$ and $\text{Var}[Z] = 35/12 \approx 2.92$. With $a = 2.5$, $\mathbb{P}[|Z - 3.5| \geq 2.5] =
\mathbb{P}[Z \in \{1, 6\}] = 1/3$, and Chebyshev gives $2.92/6.25 \approx 0.47$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Measuring the deviation in units of the standard deviation gives the form of Chebyshev's inequality that holds for every
distribution. The exercise derives it and compares it with the Gaussian.

::: {#exr-app-chebyshev-standard-deviations}
#### Deviations in standard deviations

Let $\sigma^2 = \text{Var}[Z] > 0$. Show that $\mathbb{P}[|Z - \mathbb{E}[Z]| \geq k\sigma] \leq 1/k^2$ for $k > 0$, and compare the
value at $k = 2$ with the Gaussian probability $\approx 0.046$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $a = k\sigma$ in @lem-app-chebyshev: the bound is $\sigma^2/(k\sigma)^2 = 1/k^2$. At $k = 2$ it is $0.25$, more than five times
the Gaussian value; the price of a bound valid for all distributions with finite variance.
:::
::::

Consider the random variable $\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} Z_i$. Since $Z_1, \ldots, Z_m$ are i.i.d. it is easy to verify that

$$ \text{Var}\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} Z_i\right] = \frac{\text{Var}[Z_1]}{m} $$

Applied to the empirical average, Chebyshev's inequality therefore gives a confidence interval whose width shrinks like
$1/\sqrt{m}$. The next lemma states it with confidence parameter $\delta$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-chebyshev-average}
#### Chebyshev's bound for empirical averages

Let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_m$ be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables and assume that $\mathbb{E}[Z_1] = \mu$
and $\text{Var}[Z_1] \leq 1$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then, for any $\delta \in (0,1)$, with probability of at least $1-\delta$ we have

$$ \left|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} Z_i - \mu\right| \leq \sqrt{\frac{1}{\delta m}} $$
:::

::::

The deviation between the empirical average and the mean given by Chebyshev's inequality decreases polynomially with $m$. It is
possible to obtain significantly faster, exponential decrease using Chernoff's bounds and Hoeffding's inequality.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Inverting @lem-app-chebyshev-average gives a sample size for a prescribed accuracy and confidence. The example shows how large it
is, which motivates the exponential bounds that follow.

::: {#exm-app-chebyshev-average-sample-size}
#### Sample size from Chebyshev

To guarantee accuracy $\epsilon = 0.01$ with confidence $1 - \delta = 0.95$ we need $\sqrt{1/(\delta m)} \leq \epsilon$, that is,
$m \geq 1/(\delta\epsilon^2) = 1/(0.05 \cdot 10^{-4}) = 200{,}000$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The lemma is a direct consequence of the variance identity above and Chebyshev's inequality. The exercise asks to put the two
together.

::: {#exr-app-chebyshev-average-proof}
#### Proof of the lemma

Prove @lem-app-chebyshev-average.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The average $\bar{Z}$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\text{Var}[Z_1]/m \leq 1/m$. By @lem-app-chebyshev with $a = \sqrt{1/(\delta
m)}$, $\mathbb{P}[|\bar{Z} - \mu| \geq a] \leq (1/m)/(1/(\delta m)) = \delta$, so $|\bar{Z} - \mu| < a$ with probability at least $1
- \delta$.
:::
::::

### Chernoff's Bounds

Chernoff's bounds provide exponentially decreasing tail probabilities for sums of independent Bernoulli random variables. The first
bounds the probability that the sum exceeds its mean by a factor $1 + \delta$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-chernoff-upper}
#### Chernoff bound, upper tail

Let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_m$ be independent Bernoulli variables where for every
$i$, $\mathbb{P}[Z_i = 1] = p_i$ and $\mathbb{P}[Z_i = 0] = 1 - p_i$ [@shalev2014ml]. Let $p = \sum_{i=1}^{m} p_i$ and let $Z =
\sum_{i=1}^{m} Z_i$. Then, for any $\delta > 0$,

$$ \mathbb{P}[Z > (1+\delta)p] \leq e^{-h(\delta)p} $$

where

$$ h(\delta) = (1+\delta)\log(1+\delta) - \delta $$
:::

::::

Using the inequality $h(a) \geq a^2/(2 + 2a/3)$ we obtain the simplified bound:

$$ \mathbb{P}[Z > (1+\delta)p] \leq e^{-p\frac{\delta^2}{2+2\delta/3}} $$

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The example evaluates @lem-app-chernoff-upper and its simplified form for a sum of a thousand rare events. It shows that the
simplification costs very little.

::: {#exm-app-chernoff-upper-rare-events}
#### A thousand rare events

Let $m = 1000$ and $p_i = 0.1$, so $p = 100$, and take $\delta = 0.5$. Then $h(0.5) = 1.5\log 1.5 - 0.5 \approx 0.1082$ and
$\mathbb{P}[Z > 150] \leq e^{-10.82} \approx 2.0 \times 10^{-5}$; the simplified bound gives $e^{-100 \cdot 0.25/2.333} =
e^{-10.71} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-5}$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The simplified bound is convenient for finding how large $p$ must be. The exercise checks the inequality on $h$ at one point and
then solves for $p$.

::: {#exr-app-chernoff-upper-required-mean}
#### How large must the mean be?

(a) Check $h(1) \geq 1/(2 + 2/3)$. (b) With $\delta = 0.1$, how large must $p$ be for the simplified bound to give $\mathbb{P}[Z >
1.1p] \leq 0.01$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $h(1) = 2\log 2 - 1 \approx 0.386 \geq 0.375$. (b) We need $p\delta^2/(2 + 2\delta/3) \geq \log 100 \approx 4.605$. Here
$\delta^2/(2 + 2\delta/3) = 0.01/2.0667 \approx 0.004839$, so $p \geq 4.605/0.004839 \approx 951.7$, i.e. $p \geq 952$.
:::
::::

The same method bounds the probability of falling below the mean by a factor $1 - \delta$. The next lemma shows that this lower
tail is at least as small as the upper one.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-chernoff-lower}
#### Chernoff bound, lower tail

Using the notation above, we also have [@shalev2014ml]

$$ \mathbb{P}[Z < (1-\delta)p] \leq e^{-ph(-\delta)} \leq e^{-ph(\delta)} \leq e^{-p\frac{\delta^2}{2+2\delta/3}} $$
:::

::::

These bounds show that the probability of large deviations decreases exponentially with the sample size, which is much faster than
the polynomial rate given by Chebyshev's inequality.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Returning to the thousand rare events, the lower tail can be bounded in the same way. The example shows that @lem-app-chernoff-lower
gives a noticeably smaller number than the upper tail did.

::: {#exm-app-chernoff-lower-rare-events}
#### The lower tail for the same sum

With $p = 100$ and $\delta = 0.5$, $h(-0.5) = 0.5\log 0.5 + 0.5 \approx 0.1534$, so $\mathbb{P}[Z < 50] \leq e^{-15.34} \approx 2.2
\times 10^{-7}$, compared with $2.0 \times 10^{-5}$ for $\mathbb{P}[Z > 150]$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The middle inequality of the lemma, $h(-\delta) \geq h(\delta)$, is what makes the lower tail lighter. The exercise proves it and
combines the two tails.

::: {#exr-app-chernoff-lower-comparison}
#### Comparing $h(-\delta)$ and $h(\delta)$

Show that $h(-\delta) \geq h(\delta)$ for $\delta \in (0, 1)$, and deduce $\mathbb{P}[|Z - p| > \delta p] \leq
2e^{-p\delta^2/(2 + 2\delta/3)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $g(\delta) = h(-\delta) - h(\delta) = 2\delta + (1 - \delta)\log(1 - \delta) - (1 + \delta)\log(1 + \delta)$. Then $g(0) = 0$ and
$g'(\delta) = 2 - \log(1 - \delta) - 1 - \log(1 + \delta) - 1 = -\log(1 - \delta^2) \geq 0$, so $g \geq 0$ on $(0, 1)$. The event
$|Z - p| > \delta p$ is contained in the union of $Z > (1 + \delta)p$ and $Z < (1 - \delta)p$; adding the two simplified bounds of
@lem-app-chernoff-upper and @lem-app-chernoff-lower gives the claim.
:::
::::

### Hoeffding's Inequality

Hoeffding's inequality generalizes Chernoff's bounds to arbitrary bounded random variables, not just Bernoulli variables. It is the
inequality behind most finite-class generalization bounds.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-hoeffding-inequality}
#### Hoeffding's inequality

Let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_m$ be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables and let
$\bar{Z} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} Z_i$ [@shalev2014ml]. Assume that $\mathbb{E}[\bar{Z}] = \mu$ and $\mathbb{P}[a \leq Z_i \leq
b] = 1$ for every $i$. Then, for any $\epsilon > 0$

$$ \mathbb{P}\left[\left|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} Z_i - \mu\right| > \epsilon\right] \leq
2\exp\left(-\frac{2m\epsilon^2}{(b-a)^2}\right) $$
:::

::::

This inequality is one of the most important tools in statistical learning theory. It provides a uniform bound that holds for all
$\epsilon > 0$ and shows that the probability of deviation decreases exponentially with both the sample size $m$ and the square of
the deviation $\epsilon^2$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The example compares @lem-app-hoeffding-inequality with Chebyshev's inequality for the same average of variables in $[0, 1]$. It
shows the gain of the exponential bound at a moderate sample size.

::: {#exm-app-hoeffding-inequality-versus-chebyshev}
#### Hoeffding versus Chebyshev

Let $Z_i \in [0, 1]$, $m = 1000$ and $\epsilon = 0.05$. Hoeffding gives $2e^{-2 \cdot 1000 \cdot 0.0025} = 2e^{-5} \approx 0.013$.
Since $\text{Var}[Z_i] \leq 1/4$, Chebyshev gives $(1/4)/(1000 \cdot 0.0025) = 0.1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Solving Hoeffding's bound for $m$ gives the sample size needed for a given accuracy and confidence. The exercise computes it and
compares it with the Chebyshev sample size of @exm-app-chebyshev-average-sample-size.

::: {#exr-app-hoeffding-inequality-sample-size}
#### Sample size from Hoeffding

Show that $m \geq (b - a)^2\log(2/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2)$ guarantees $|\bar{Z} - \mu| \leq \epsilon$ with probability at least $1 -
\delta$, and evaluate it for $[a, b] = [0, 1]$, $\epsilon = 0.01$, $\delta = 0.05$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The bound $2\exp(-2m\epsilon^2/(b - a)^2) \leq \delta$ is equivalent to $m \geq (b - a)^2\log(2/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2)$. Here
$\log 40 \approx 3.689$ and $m \geq 3.689/(2 \cdot 10^{-4}) \approx 18{,}444.4$, so $m = 18{,}445$ suffices, against $200{,}000$ from
@lem-app-chebyshev-average.
:::
::::

Hoeffding's inequality is proved by bounding the moment generating function of each bounded summand. The next lemma is that bound.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#lem-app-hoeffding-lemma}
#### Hoeffding's lemma

Let $X$ be a random variable that takes values in the interval $[a,b]$ and such
that $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$ [@shalev2014ml]. Then, for every $\lambda > 0$,

$$ \mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X}] \leq e^{\frac{\lambda^2(b-a)^2}{8}} $$
:::

::::

This technical lemma is the key ingredient in proving Hoeffding's inequality and demonstrates how moment generating functions can
be bounded for bounded random variables.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a random sign the moment generating function is a hyperbolic cosine, so @lem-app-hoeffding-lemma can be compared with
@lem-app-cosh-gaussian-bound. The two give the same bound.

::: {#exm-app-hoeffding-lemma-rademacher}
#### A random sign

Let $X = \pm 1$ with probability $1/2$ each, so $[a, b] = [-1, 1]$ and $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$. Then $\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X}] =
\cosh\lambda$, and the lemma gives $e^{\lambda^2 \cdot 4/8} = e^{\lambda^2/2}$, which is exactly @lem-app-cosh-gaussian-bound.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercise derives one half of Hoeffding's inequality from Hoeffding's lemma and Markov's inequality. This is the Chernoff method,
the same argument used for random signs in @exr-app-cosh-gaussian-bound-rademacher.

::: {#exr-app-hoeffding-lemma-to-inequality}
#### From the lemma to the inequality

In the setting of @lem-app-hoeffding-inequality, show that $\mathbb{P}[\bar{Z} - \mu > \epsilon] \leq \exp(-2m\epsilon^2/(b -
a)^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $X_i = (Z_i - \mu)/m$ has mean zero and lies in an interval of length $(b - a)/m$. For $\lambda > 0$, @lem-app-markov applied to
$e^{\lambda(\bar{Z} - \mu)}$, independence and @lem-app-hoeffding-lemma give
$$ \mathbb{P}[\bar{Z} - \mu > \epsilon] \leq e^{-\lambda\epsilon}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X_i}] \leq
e^{-\lambda\epsilon + \lambda^2(b - a)^2/(8m)}. $$
Choosing $\lambda = 4m\epsilon/(b - a)^2$ makes the exponent $-4m\epsilon^2/(b - a)^2 + 2m\epsilon^2/(b - a)^2 = -2m\epsilon^2/(b -
a)^2$. Applying the same argument to $-Z_i$ and adding gives the factor $2$ of the two-sided inequality.
:::
::::

### Applications to Learning Theory

These concentration inequalities have direct applications in learning theory:

- **Uniform Convergence**: Hoeffding's inequality combined with union bounds provides uniform convergence guarantees for finite
hypothesis classes.
- **Sample Complexity**: The exponential decay rate determines how many samples are needed to achieve a
desired accuracy with high probability.
- **Generalization Bounds**: These inequalities bound the difference between training
error and test error, providing theoretical guarantees for learning algorithms.

The transition from polynomial (Chebyshev) to exponential (Hoeffding) concentration is crucial for obtaining practical sample
complexity bounds in PAC learning.

## Exercises {#sec-appendices-and-technical-background-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The integrative exercises below combine the three sections of the chapter: technical lemmas, linear algebra and concentration. The
first one bounds a random linear combination of signs, using the hyperbolic cosine bound, Markov's inequality and the Euclidean
norm.

::: {#exr-app-int-rademacher-combination}
#### Random linear combinations of signs

Let $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_m$ be independent random signs, $\mathbb{P}[\sigma_i = \pm 1] = 1/2$, and let $\mathbf{w} \in
\mathbb{R}^m$ be nonzero.
(a) Using @lem-app-cosh-gaussian-bound, show that $\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\sigma_i w_i}] \leq e^{\lambda^2 w_i^2/2}$.
(b) Using @lem-app-markov, show that $\mathbb{P}[\sum_i w_i\sigma_i \geq t] \leq e^{-\lambda t}\prod_i \mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda
w_i\sigma_i}]$ for $\lambda > 0$.
(c) Express the result through the norm of @def-app-inner-product-norms: show $\mathbb{P}[\langle \mathbf{w}, \boldsymbol{\sigma}
\rangle \geq t] \leq e^{-t^2/(2\|\mathbf{w}\|^2)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda w_i\sigma_i}] = \cosh(\lambda w_i) \leq e^{\lambda^2 w_i^2/2}$ by @lem-app-cosh-gaussian-bound with $a =
\lambda w_i$.
(b) $e^{\lambda S}$, with $S = \sum_i w_i\sigma_i$, is nonnegative, and $S \geq t$ iff $e^{\lambda S} \geq e^{\lambda t}$. By
@lem-app-markov and independence, $\mathbb{P}[S \geq t] \leq e^{-\lambda t}\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda S}] = e^{-\lambda t}\prod_i
\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda w_i\sigma_i}]$.
(c) Combining, $\mathbb{P}[\langle \mathbf{w}, \boldsymbol{\sigma} \rangle \geq t] \leq e^{-\lambda t + \lambda^2\sum_i w_i^2/2} =
e^{-\lambda t + \lambda^2\|\mathbf{w}\|^2/2}$. Minimising over $\lambda$ at $\lambda = t/\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$ gives
$e^{-t^2/(2\|\mathbf{w}\|^2)}$.
:::

The second exercise derives a sample size for a finite hypothesis class. It combines Hoeffding's inequality with a range bound from
linear algebra and with the logarithm lemma that makes an implicit sample size explicit.

::: {#exr-app-int-finite-class-sample-size}
#### Sample size for a finite class

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite set of $N$ hypotheses, and let $L_S(h)$ be the average loss of $h$ on $m$ i.i.d. examples and $L_D(h)$
its expectation.
(a) If the loss takes values in $[0, 1]$, use @lem-app-hoeffding-inequality and a union bound to show that $m \geq \log(2N/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2)$
guarantees $|L_S(h) - L_D(h)| \leq \epsilon$ for all $h \in \mathcal{H}$ simultaneously, with probability at least $1 - \delta$.
(b) Let the hypotheses be linear predictors $\mathbf{x} \mapsto \langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle$ with $\|\mathbf{w}\| \leq 1$,
the inputs satisfy $\|\mathbf{x}\| \leq 1$, the labels $|y| \leq 1$, and the loss be $(\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle - y)^2$.
Show that the loss lies in $[0, 4]$ and restate the sample size of (a).
(c) Suppose, back in the setting of (a), that $N = m^d$ grows with $m$. Use @lem-app-log-versus-linear-offset to give an explicit
sufficient $m$, and evaluate it for $d = 5$, $\epsilon = 0.1$, $\delta = 0.05$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) For each $h$, @lem-app-hoeffding-inequality with $b - a = 1$ gives $\mathbb{P}[|L_S(h) - L_D(h)| > \epsilon] \leq 2e^{-2m\epsilon^2}$.
By the union bound the probability that some $h$ fails is at most $2Ne^{-2m\epsilon^2}$, which is at most $\delta$ iff $m \geq
\log(2N/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2)$.
(b) By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $|\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle| \leq \|\mathbf{w}\|\|\mathbf{x}\| \leq 1$, so
$|\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle - y| \leq 2$ and the loss lies in $[0, 4]$. With $(b - a)^2 = 16$ the condition becomes $m
\geq 16\log(2N/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2) = 8\log(2N/\delta)/\epsilon^2$.
(c) The condition reads $m \geq a\log(m) + b$ with $a = d/(2\epsilon^2)$ and $b = \log(2/\delta)/(2\epsilon^2)$. For $d \geq 1$ and
$\epsilon \leq 1/\sqrt{2}$ we have $a \geq 1$, and $b > 0$ for $\delta < 2$, so the lemma gives the sufficient condition $m \geq
4a\log(2a) + 2b$. For the given values, $a = 250$, $b = \log 40/0.02 \approx 184.4$ and $4a\log(2a) + 2b = 1000\log 500 + 368.9
\approx 6214.6 + 368.9 = 6583.5$, so $m = 6584$ suffices. Directly, $250\log 6584 + 184.4 \approx 2198.1 + 184.4 = 2382.5 \leq
6584$.
:::

The third exercise bounds the projection of a random vector onto a direction. It uses the spectral decomposition to control a
variance, Chebyshev's inequality to bound the tail, and the expectation lemma for sub-Gaussian tails to bound the mean.

::: {#exr-app-int-projection-tails}
#### Projections of a random vector

Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a random vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}] = \mathbf{0}$ and covariance $\Sigma =
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}]$, and let $\mathbf{u}$ be a unit vector.
(a) Show that $\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite and, using @thm-app-spectral-decomposition, that $\text{Var}[\langle \mathbf{u},
\mathbf{x} \rangle] = \langle \mathbf{u}, \Sigma\mathbf{u} \rangle \leq \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)$.
(b) Use @lem-app-chebyshev to bound $\mathbb{P}[|\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{x} \rangle| \geq a]$.
(c) Now let the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ be independent random signs. Using @exr-app-int-rademacher-combination, show that the
hypothesis of @lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation holds for $X = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{x} \rangle$, $x' = 0$, $a = \sqrt{2}$,
and compare its conclusion with the bound $\mathbb{E}[|X|] \leq \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]}$ from (a).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\Sigma$ is symmetric and $\langle \mathbf{v}, \Sigma\mathbf{v} \rangle = \mathbb{E}[\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{x} \rangle^2]
\geq 0$, so it is positive semidefinite by @thm-app-psd-characterizations. Since $\mathbb{E}[\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{x} \rangle]
= 0$, $\text{Var}[\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{x} \rangle] = \mathbb{E}[\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{x} \rangle^2] = \langle
\mathbf{u}, \Sigma\mathbf{u} \rangle$. Writing $\Sigma = \sum_i \lambda_i\mathbf{u}_i\mathbf{u}_i^{\top}$, this equals $\sum_i
\lambda_i\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u}_i \rangle^2 \leq \lambda_{\max}\sum_i \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u}_i \rangle^2 =
\lambda_{\max}\|\mathbf{u}\|^2 = \lambda_{\max}$.
(b) By @lem-app-chebyshev, $\mathbb{P}[|\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{x} \rangle| \geq a] \leq \lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)/a^2$.
(c) With random-sign coordinates, @exr-app-int-rademacher-combination with $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u}$ gives $\mathbb{P}[X \geq t] \leq
e^{-t^2/2}$, and since $-\mathbf{x}$ has the same distribution as $\mathbf{x}$, also $\mathbb{P}[X \leq -t] \leq e^{-t^2/2}$. Hence
$\mathbb{P}[|X| > t] \leq 2e^{-t^2/2} = 2e^{-t^2/a^2}$ with $a = \sqrt{2}$, and @lem-app-subgaussian-tail-expectation gives
$\mathbb{E}[|X|] \leq 4\sqrt{2} \approx 5.66$. Here $\Sigma = I$, so (a) gives $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = 1$ and $\mathbb{E}[|X|] \leq 1$:
the lemma trades sharpness for needing only a tail bound. (For comparison, (b) gives $1/a^2$ while the exponential tail gives
$2e^{-a^2/2}$, e.g. $0.11$ versus $0.022$ at $a = 3$.)
:::
::::
